summary: CycloShield-MZ is a web prototype that turns cyclone forecasts into earlier, fairer warnings for Mozambique. Using Cyclone Freddy (2023) as a case study, it combines open data (NASA GPM rainfall, NOAA sea surface temperature and best-track records) to show the warm-water “fuel” in the Mozambique Channel, compares the predicted track with the real one, and measures forecast error by lead time. That error becomes a safety margin: instead of warning only districts under the predicted path, the app also flags those within the typical forecast error and classifies each district as direct impact, alert or watch. It then generates short SMS messages and a simulated USSD menu for basic phones, with risk level and estimated arrival time. Cyclones repeatedly devastate Mozambique, and a warning that arrives late, in the wrong place or without internet costs lives. We cannot stop a cyclone, but we can reduce its impact.
details:
What it does and how it works
CycloShield-MZ is a Streamlit web app with four views, built around the Freddy case study:

  • Radar & Ocean Fuel: maps sea surface temperature with the 28 °C isotherm, accumulated rainfall, the real and predicted cyclone tracks, and the forecast error (in km) by lead time.
  • Risk by Region: classifies each district by its distance to the predicted track. Within a damage radius R is “direct impact”; within R plus the historical forecast error is “alert”; within R plus twice the error is “watch”. A backtest compares the districts actually hit with the districts warned, with and without the error margin. An exposure index combines proximity and rainfall; it is a relative index, not a probability.
  • What-if Simulator: an illustrative tool showing how maximum wind could change with cooler seas. It uses an explicit, editable linear assumption and is not an operational forecast.
  • Community Alert: generates short SMS messages with the region, risk level and estimated arrival time, plus a simulated USSD menu. It includes a character counter, because accented characters cut an SMS from 160 to 70 characters.

Benefits
Warnings that account for forecast uncertainty, so communities near the edge of an uncertain path are not left out. The app works fully offline, because it reads only local data files. The messages are designed for basic phones without internet. The method is transparent: every parameter (damage radius, margin, sensitivity) is visible and editable.

Intended impact
A decision-support tool for authorities such as INGD and INAM, and for the communities they serve, giving earlier and better-targeted warnings. In the short term it is a prototype validated on one real event. In the medium term we would calibrate and test it on other cyclones (Idai, Chido) and pilot it in one district. In the long term the approach could be replicated in neighbouring countries exposed to the same cyclones.

Tools, languages and data
Python, Streamlit, Plotly, pandas, NumPy, xarray and NetCDF, Zarr and s3fs, Git and GitHub, and a landing page and slides for presentation. Data: NASA GPM IMERG rainfall (read from a public Zarr store), NOAA OISST v2.1 sea surface temperature, IBTrACS best-track data (NOAA), Natural Earth coastlines and geoBoundaries district boundaries. Forecast positions are entered from public tropical cyclone advisories.

Creative aspect
We treat forecast uncertainty as part of the warning itself, rather than as a problem to hide, and we measure it on a real case. We focus on the “last mile”: a warning only matters if it reaches someone with a basic phone. The maps are drawn on longitude/latitude axes with no web map tiles, so the whole app works offline during a power or internet failure.

Factors our team considered

  • Scientific honesty: the error margin is calibrated and tested on the same cyclone (Freddy), so the results are a demonstration, not a validation. The what-if simulator is illustrative. The exposure index is not a probability.
  • Data access: sea surface temperature comes from NOAA, not NASA, because the NASA MUR service was not reachable from our network. The rainfall data is NASA GPM.
  • Languages: we avoided machine translation for Sena and Makhuwa, which need validation by native speakers before any real use.
  • Real-world deployment: USSD requires a short code, agreements with mobile operators and the regulator, and an institutional mandate. USSD is also a pull channel (people dial in), so SMS or cell broadcast would carry the alert, and USSD would let people consult their risk. In this prototype, USSD is simulated.
  • Scope: a single developer and 48 hours, so we prioritised a working end-to-end flow over breadth.
